**Put the model on trial before using it.** A near-perfect fit to last year's headcount curve is not validation.

**Why the fit proves little.** With six free parameters, you can usually bend a model to match one curve. The fit shows the parameters were adjusted well. It doesn't show the model has the right structure. Several different structures can produce the same history and then diverge sharply under a reorganization. A reorg is the kind of change the model has never seen, because it changes the structure itself.

**What to do first, in order:**

1. **Write down what would prove the model wrong, before running anything.** For example: "If the model predicts X under the reorg and the managers who run those teams say Y, we don't trust it." Setting this up front guards against confirmation bias.
2. **Run a structural trial, separate from the fit.**
   - Take each link in the model, such as attrition, hiring lag and span of control. Ask someone who works where that link lives, ideally someone who didn't build the model, to point to the real mechanism and defend it.
   - Record any link that exists only because it improved the fit.
   - Keep this verdict separate from the fit. A good fit doesn't excuse an indefensible link.
3. **Check which parameters were tuned.**
   - List the six parameters and note which ones have ever been measured rather than just fitted.
   - Hold out data if you can. Test the model on a different year or a different business unit that it wasn't tuned on.
4. **Run sensitivity analysis against the actual decision.**
   - Frame the decision as a margin between options, such as reorg design A versus B.
   - Swing each shaky parameter ±25% one at a time and see whether the recommendation flips. Draw it as a tornado chart.
   - Because the six were tuned together, they may be wrong together. A one-at-a-time test can't show that, so follow up with a Sobol analysis if the model runs in code.
5. **Produce a measurement to-do list.** Name the parameter that, if measured directly, would most change your confidence in the recommendation.

**What the outcome means.** If the structure holds up and the recommendation survives the sensitivity runs, use the model, and state which parameters the advice depends on. If it doesn't, treat the model as a way to explore questions rather than a forecaster, and measure the flagged parameters before committing to the reorg.

I haven't run anything here, since I don't have the model or the data. This is the procedure from the systems-thinking skill's "validate a model" and "one-at-a-time swing test" cards. If you share the model, I can help set up the swing test.
